messages.subject: Re: 'cores' argument
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

I'm not sure if what I am experiencing is exactly the same issue mentioned by Selcan but I have noted that scan1 and scan1perm code see to run ~5-10 time slower on HPC compared.
This is even when the cores are set to core=1. (With higher cores I run into problems with  high memory utilisation. So it is more efficient for me to set cores=1 and write my own code for clustering)

A scan which takes 1 minute on my personal computer takes about 10 minutes on on the cluster.

I've asked the people who run the cluster service to have a look at the idea and so far they haven't been able to figure how to address this.

Not sure that it is something that you will be able to help with as it may be something specific about our cluster set up. But I am curious to know if others have had any issues running there code on a cluster and whether they have any tips!

Cheers
Senthil

messages.subject: Re: 'cores' argument
messages.body_plain:
Could you say more about the operating system on your cluster?

There are two methods for parallel computing in R. R/qtl2 mostly uses mclapply(), but it can also use parLapply() if you first run makeCluster() to create a cluster object and then use that with the cores argument.

       https://github.com/rqtl/qtl2/blob/master/R/cluster_util.R#L39-L51

It seems like the mclapply() method is not sharing memory they way it should, but rather duplicating objects.

karl

messages.subject: Re: 'cores' argument
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

Thanks for the quick response.

The cluster runs CentOS’ v6.9.

I should clarify that there are two issues I have noted.

1)The memory issues when using multiple cores with the "core= ..." argument. This is not specific to the the HPC cluster. Seems to occur on windows PC when running the analysis with core= 2+. I have a work around for this which basically involves using clusterapply to run scan1 or scan1perm with 3-4 chromosomes at a time across multiple phenotypes. This way I can use all cores on our PC without exceeding the available memory.

The second issue which is really puzzling me is the fact that the both the scan1 and scan1perm codes seem to be run 5-10x slower on our HPC cluster compared to a windows PC with core=1. This does not seem to be a problem with clustering but some other clash perhaps with the code and maybe the cluster set up.

Thanks

Senthil

messages.subject: R/qtl2 is now on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
R/qtl2 is now on CRAN <https://cran.r-project.org>, and so you can install it with

    install.packages("qtl2")

You can update to the latest version with

    update.packages()

The latest release is version 0.22-11. It is not materially different from version 0.22; there were just a bunch of small changes in the documentation to conform to CRAN rules.

karl

messages.subject: Cleaning genoprobs prior to scan1
messages.body_plain:
Hello Karl and others,

I was wondering what your recommendations were with using the clean_genoprobs() function before running any genome scan with scan1.

>From what I understand extremely small probabilities can result in more unusually high coefficients with scan1 coef. I also assume since scan1 is fitting regression model to obtain RSS values which is then used to calculate LOD scores. LOD scores will also be affected by these small probabilities.

When I test this I do see that the lod curves after cleaning seem much smoother. Without these spikes which i assume is due to the small probabilities.

I don't see any real downside with using the clean function to get rid of these extremely small probabilities.

Thanks
Senthil

messages.subject: Permutation for Distant / Trans Associations
messages.body_plain:
Hi I was wondering if the permutation statistic can also be applied for distant / trans associations. Many researchers have told me that distant effects require more stringent LOD cutoffs. I was wondering if there is a means to empirically derive this? I am working with the DO mouse line.

Thanks

messages.subject: Re: Permutation for Distant / Trans Associations
messages.body_plain:
The typical permutation approach is adjusting for the scan across the genome but only considering a single trait. You could use a similar approach to control the family-wise error rate in the search across both the genome and across multiple phenotypes. Alternatively, you could control the family-wise error rate for the genome scan of a phenotype, but then control the false discovery rate in the search across phenotypes, for example with the qvalue package <https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/qvalue.html>.

karl

messages.body_plain:

Thank you for your help previously.

I have been examining cage effects for DO phenotypes. Using cage as an additive covariate, I expected to observe differences in regions associated with particular phenotypes, although association strengths appear to vary widely genome-wide.

Would you please be able to explain how scan1 uses additive covariates?

Kind regards,

Harry

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Covariates and scan1
messages.body_plain:
We fit a model like

     y = a G + b X + e

where G = genotype probabilities for a position
X = additive covariates

If there are interactive covariates, there will also be terms c (z G) for each interactive covariate column z.

karl
